fp.fragment: first-class function objects and closures; mutation is allowed
fp.why: Callbacks and pipelines are how the host multiplexes I/O and UI.
fp.useWhen: Array methods, event handlers, and any API that takes a function value.
fp.price: Mutable closed-over state and call-site this-binding are the tax.

sources.quote: A programming language is said to have First-class functions when functions in that language are treated like any other variable.
It has dynamic typing, prototype-based object-orientation, and first-class functions.

oop.fragment: prototypal objects plus class syntax over the same object model
oop.why: Domain models and UI widgets are still object-shaped in most codebases.
oop.useWhen: Widgets, services, and any API that expects new/class.
oop.price: this is call-site bound; mixing prototypes and class sugar confuses readers.

sources.quote: ECMAScript is an object-oriented programming language for performing computations and manipulating computational objects within a host environment.
JavaScript is a prototype-based language — an object's behaviors are specified by its own properties and its prototype's properties.

decl.fragment: imperative statements and expressions; declaration is a framework dialect
decl.why: The core language evaluates statements, not a specification engine.

sources.quote: It is multi-paradigm, supporting event-driven, functional, and imperative programming styles.
JavaScript is a scripting language that enables you to create dynamically updating content, control multimedia, animate images, and pretty much everything else.

decl.reason: Imperative core. JSX/templates compile to calls; they are not the language.

actor.fragment: no mailbox actor runtime in the language
actor.why: Workers are host isolates with postMessage, not supervised actors.

sources.quote: Workers (as these background scripts are called herein) are relatively heavy-weight, and are not intended to be used in large numbers.
Web Workers makes it possible to run a script operation in a background thread separate from the main execution thread of a web application.

actor.reason: Workers are isolate scripts with structured-clone handoff, not an actor/OTP runtime.

static.fragment: dynamic: values are tagged at runtime; no compile-time checker in the language
static.why: The web needed source that runs without a compile step.
static.useWhen: Any program that must run in an engine with no ahead-of-time checker.
static.price: TypeError shows up in production; undefined is not a function.

sources.quote: Dynamically-typed languages are those (like JavaScript) where the interpreter assigns variables a type at runtime based on the variable's value at the time.
JavaScript only truly provides dynamic typing - running the code to see what happens.

strong.fragment: weak coercions on == and ToPrimitive; === still exists
strong.why: Loose equality was a 1995 convenience frozen by the web.
strong.useWhen: Always; prefer strict equality in new code.
strong.price: Implicit conversions hide bugs; linters exist because the language will not.

sources.quote: Double equals (==) will perform a type conversion when comparing two things, and will handle NaN, -0, and +0 specially to conform to IEEE 754
Values are cast to numbers by casting to strings and then casting the strings to numbers.

hm.fragment: no Hindley–Milner; there is no language type inference algorithm
hm.why: Types are runtime tags, not inferred schemes.

sources.quote: It was first implemented as part of the type system of the programming language ML.

hm.reason: No HM. Inference, if any, lives in a separate typed language.

dep.fragment: no dependent types; the language types are a closed runtime set
dep.why: The engine manipulates a fixed set of tagged values.

sources.quote: The ECMAScript language types are Undefined, Null, Boolean, String, Symbol, Number, BigInt, and Object.
In computer science and logic, a dependent type is a type whose definition depends on a value.

dep.reason: No Π/Σ types. The language types are a closed runtime set.

gen.fragment: no type parameters in the language
gen.why: Reuse is duck-typed objects and functions, not parametric types.

sources.quote: The ECMAScript language types are Undefined, Null, Boolean, String, Symbol, Number, BigInt, and Object.
We say that this version of the identity function is generic, as it works over a range of types.

gen.reason: No generics in the language. Parametric types are a compile-time layer elsewhere.

sources.quote: JavaScript automatically allocates memory when objects are created and frees it when they are not used anymore (garbage collection).
Users of JavaScript don’t have direct access to the garbage collector; it is totally implementation-defined.

malloc.reason: No malloc/free in the language. The engine allocates and collects.

gc.fragment: engine tracing GC; authors never free ordinary objects
gc.why: Short-lived object graphs dominate page and server heaps.
gc.useWhen: All ordinary heaps in this language.
gc.price: Pause and heap size are not under app control; no deterministic destruction.

sources.quote: JavaScript automatically allocates memory when objects are created and frees it when they are not used anymore (garbage collection).
The major GC collects garbage from the entire heap. Major GC happens in three phases: marking, sweeping and compacting.

trace.fragment: generational scavenger plus old-generation mark-compact in typical engines
trace.why: Most objects die young; a nursery matches that mortality.
trace.price: You profile; you do not pick the algorithm from source.

sources.quote: There is a young generation (split further into ‘nursery’ and ‘intermediate’ sub-generations), and an old generation.
JavaScript automatically allocates memory when objects are created and frees it when they are not used anymore (garbage collection).

rc.fragment: engines trace; they do not expose ARC
rc.why: Reachability, not retain counts, is the published model.

sources.quote: Garbage collectors do this by using reachability as a proxy for ‘liveness’.
JavaScript automatically allocates memory when objects are created and frees it when they are not used anymore (garbage collection).

rc.reason: Not reference counting as the heap. Engines trace reachable objects.

own.fragment: no borrow checker; the collector owns lifetime
own.why: Alias-freedom is not a type-system property here.

sources.quote: JavaScript automatically allocates memory when objects are created and frees it when they are not used anymore (garbage collection).
JavaScript is a high-level, often just-in-time–compiled language that conforms to the ECMAScript standard.

own.reason: No affine types or borrow checker. GC owns lifetime.

thr.fragment: one agent thread per isolate; workers do not share the language heap by default
thr.why: The UI/agent thread cannot block on a second mutator in the same heap.

sources.quote: The event loop is what allows Node.js to perform non-blocking I/O operations — despite the fact that a single JavaScript thread is used by default
An agent is a thread, which means the interpreter can only process one statement at a time.

thr.reason: No shared-memory thread-plus-mutex model as the language default. Workers are separate agents.

coro.fragment: async functions and await over promises
coro.why: I/O without a thread per request on a single agent.
coro.useWhen: Network, timers, and UI idle work.
coro.price: Awaiting still occupies the agent until the turn ends; blocking the turn freezes it.

sources.quote: The async function declaration creates a binding of a new async function to a given name. The await keyword is permitted within the function body

csp.fragment: no channels in the language; postMessage is isolate handoff
csp.why: Handoff is structured clone or SAB, not CSP select.

sources.quote: The Worker() constructor call creates a worker and returns a Worker object representing that worker, which is used to communicate with the worker.
Web Workers makes it possible to run a script operation in a background thread separate from the main execution thread of a web application.

csp.reason: No CSP channels in the language. Queues in libraries do not count.

loop.fragment: host event loop: tasks and microtasks on a single agent
loop.why: The page/server multiplexes I/O without blocking the agent.
loop.useWhen: Timers, I/O, rendering, and promise reactions.
loop.price: One blocked turn freezes that agent.

sources.quote: this is known in HTML (and also commonly) as the event loop which enables asynchronous programming in JavaScript while being single-threaded.
